topic: raising a first oak cask: jointing the staves, steaming them round and driving the hoops

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-3)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: termometr na skrzyni parowej

base: I am raising my first oak cask and the staves refuse to sit close together.
A small firkin stands finished in the corner, made by the old cooper years ago.
I hung a steam thermometer on the chest, because guessing the heat split two staves already.
The gaps show worst at the middle, where the bilge should be at its widest.
Should I redress the stave edges, or is the trouble in how I raise them?
Redress the edges first, because a cask with poor joints will never draw tight afterwards.
Each stave needs a hollow back, a bulged front and edges cut to a bevel.
That bevel must change along the length, wider at the bilge than at the head.
Work the jointer plane slowly and check every stave against its neighbour.
I rejointed all the staves and they now stand close from head to bilge.
The steam thermometer held near ninety degrees for the full half hour of heating.
Two staves cracked along the grain as I drew the truss hoop down.
Was the oak too dry, or did I pull the hoop too fast?
You pulled too fast, since oak at ninety degrees bends willingly but only over time.
Draw the truss hoop a hand's breadth, then wait and let the fibres yield.
Wet the outside as you go, so the heat travels through the whole thickness.
A stave that cracks has been asked to move faster than its grain allows.
I drew the hoop slowly over an hour and every stave came round unbroken.
The steam thermometer stayed above eighty until the last hoop was finally home.
That small firkin in the corner has far more hoops than my cask does.
Do smaller vessels need closer hooping, or was that simply the cooper's habit?
Smaller vessels do need closer hooping, because short staves flex more for a given load.
A firkin carries the same pressure as a hogshead across much less timber.
Six hoops on a firkin and eight on a barrel is the usual rule.
Set the quarter hoops before the bilge hoops, or the shape will run out.
I set the quarter hoops first and the cask now holds a fair, even bilge.
The chime is cut and the croze grooved ready for the head boards.
My head boards are dowelled but I have not yet fitted any flag between them.
Is river flag really necessary, or will a tight dowelled joint hold on its own?
Fit the flag, because no dowelled joint in a head stays tight through a winter.
Dried river flag swells the moment liquid touches it and seals the seam completely.
Lay it in the dowel joints and trim it flush with the head.
Coopers have used the same rush for centuries and nothing modern beats it.
I laid river flag through both head joints and drove the heads into the croze.
The cask held water overnight with only a slight weep near one chime.
By morning the weep had stopped entirely and the staves felt swollen and tight.
Should I trust it now, or leave it standing full for another week?
Leave it standing full, because a new cask needs a fortnight to settle properly.
Every joint takes up at its own pace and the last ones are slowest.
Check the hoops after a week and drive any that have gone slack.
After that the cask will serve you for thirty years with very little attention.
